description: Compare the Kelvin and Celsius scales in a single shared frame. Preserve the source integer correspondences 0 K/-273 degrees Celsius, 273 K/0 degrees Celsius and 373 K/100 degrees Celsius, with equal-size temperature intervals on both parallel scales. Scale spacing is regularized to the stated integer values, not measured scan distances. English headers, K without a degree sign and the explicit Integer approximation note are justified modern additions or notation corrections supported by the complete current n15 text. No extra temperature values, minor ticks, force arrows, physical apparatus or precision claims are introduced. Independent review and promotion remain separate.

authoritativeText.text:
15. Absolute temperature

Bodies can reach very high temperatures①.
For a fixed amount of ideal gas at constant pressure, raising the temperature increases the volume;
lowering the temperature decreases it.

The straight-line relation in Gay-Lussac's law (2-5) cannot be extended arbitrarily to negative volumes.
Extending this relation toward lower temperatures identifies a temperature zero point.

This uses the ideal-gas model;
it does not mean a real gas always stays gaseous while cooling to that point.

① The original textbook uses temperatures of billions of degrees as examples of very high temperatures and mentions that some stars may be hotter inside.
These examples do not establish that a particular process has reached the highest temperature in nature.

At constant pressure, extending the ideal gas's volume-temperature relation to zero volume gives the zero point called absolute zero.
Such an extension beyond the measured range is called extrapolation.
A real gas may first become a liquid or solid as it cools.

Matter still takes up space at absolute zero.
Zero volume on this extrapolated graph is a result of the model, not a real-gas cooling experiment that can be carried out directly.

A dilute gas has particles spread far apart.
In suitable temperature and pressure ranges, it can behave approximately like an ideal gas.

Measurements on increasingly dilute gases, compared through their volume-temperature relations, can identify the limiting zero point of the ideal-gas temperature scale.
Being dilute and approaching low temperature are not the same condition.

If the same real gas keeps cooling, it can depart from ideal-gas behavior.
It need not remain gaseous and actually shrink to zero volume.

Using the textbook's integer approximation, set the ideal-gas volume $V$ in equation (2-5) equal to zero and use the approximate expansion coefficient $\alpha=\frac{1}{273}$ degree$^{-1}$:
$0=V_0\left(1+\frac{1}{273}t\right)$.

This finds a zero point from a linear relation;
it does not measure a real gas's volume as zero.

This gives the approximate Celsius temperature of absolute zero, $t=-273^\circ\mathrm{C}$①.
Absolute zero is the lower limit of the ordinary thermal-equilibrium temperature scale.

In thermal equilibrium, parts that can exchange heat have the same temperature.
There is no overall flow of heat between them.
The textbook quotes Lomonosov's phrase "the final degree of cold" to describe this limit.

The integer value here is approximate.

① The Celsius temperature of absolute zero is $-273.15^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

The British scholar Kelvin established an absolute temperature scale.
Its zero point is absolute zero, and the size of a temperature interval is the same as on the Celsius scale.
The kelvin's unit symbol is K, with no degree sign.

Below, $T$ is the numerical value of temperature in K, and $t$ is its numerical value in degrees Celsius.
With this lesson's integer approximation:

$T=t+273$.
(2-6)

This equation converts numerical values between scales;
a Celsius temperature value cannot simply be used as a kelvin value.
Use the zero-point value in the footnote for the exact conversion.

Figure $22$ compares the zero points and corresponding marks on the two scales.
It uses the same integer approximation as the text.
Marks at the same height represent the same temperature, not equal numerical values on the two scales.

Classical kinetic theory is the model used here to describe the gas particles' motion.
Kinetic energy is energy of motion.
In this model, absolute temperature is related to the average kinetic energy of the gas particles' irregular motion.

As $T=0$ is approached as a limit, the average thermal kinetic energy in this classical model approaches zero.
Microscopic motion means motion on a scale too small to see directly.
This does not justify saying that all microscopic motion in every material stops completely.

The third chapter discusses temperature and microscopic motion further.

With the kelvin scale, the constant-pressure relation for a fixed amount of ideal gas has a simpler form.
Here the expansion-coefficient symbol, alpha, means just the coefficient's number: one divided by two hundred seventy-three.
This is its number when the coefficient is expressed per kelvin or per degree Celsius of temperature difference.

The physical coefficient still has its inverse-temperature unit.
These numerical equations use only its number.
Using the same integer approximation:
$1+\alpha t=1+\frac{1}{273}(T-273)=\alpha T$.

Therefore:
$V=V_0\alpha T$.
(2-7)

These equations use the temperature and coefficient values just specified.
For a fixed amount of gas at fixed pressure, volume is proportional to absolute temperature.

Figure 22

Thus, for a fixed amount of ideal gas in two states at the same pressure, the volume ratio equals the absolute-temperature ratio:
$\frac{V_1}{V_2}=\frac{T_1}{T_2}$.
(2-8)

Both temperatures must use the same kelvin scale, and the denominator temperature must be positive.
Do not substitute Celsius numerical values directly into this ratio.

inventory.description: The reopened original has two narrow solid outlined vertical scales, Kelvin on the left and Celsius on the right. Both extend above their top labelled tick and end at the shared bottom reference. Kelvin ticks face left, Celsius ticks face right. Three paired levels, from bottom to top, are 0/-273, 273/0 and 373/100. The top two pairs have short solid tick strokes, not connecting dashed horizontal lines. Source integers are approximate; exact equal-unit spacing is a modern regularization of these same integer values, not a measured geometry claim.

The source Chinese headers name the Kelvin and Celsius temperature scales. Kelvin labels are to the left: 373, 273 and 0, each printed with old degree-K notation. Celsius labels are to the right: 100, 0 and -273, each with degree-C notation. Modern English headers replace Chinese wording and the obsolete degree sign is removed from K, while every integer, sign, side and correspondence is preserved. No more precise replacement numbers are inserted.

One horizontal dashed line extends across the bottom beneath both scales, linking the 0 K and -273 Celsius levels and continuing beyond each scale. The scale outlines and other ticks are solid. Preserve this single dashed reference, without adding dashed guides at the two higher pairs.

Justified modern addition, not source pixels: Integer approximation explicitly identifies the rounded integer conversion used in the current n15 lesson and this source figure. It does not claim that 273 or -273 is the exact modern offset. No new conversion formula or additional numerical label is added.
